Definition — Linear, sublinear and quadratic convergence
      
        Nonnegative errors $e_k\to0$ converge linearly (geometrically) with rate $q\in(0,1)$ if $e_{k+1}\le q\,e_k$, so $e_k\le q^ke_0$; sublinearly if slower than every geometric rate, for example $e_k=C/k^p$ with $C,p\gt0$ and $k\ge1$ (a polynomial upper bound alone does not rule out geometric convergence); quadratically if $e_{k+1}\le Ce_k^2$ with $C\gt0$ (scalar Newton's method near a regular root of a $C^2$ function, from a sufficiently close initial point).

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: Nonnegative errors with the one-step geometric inequality have every prefix bounded by q^k e0 and converge to zero.
hypotheses: error:N->R; all errors nonnegative; 0<=q<1; error(n+1)<=q*error(n) for every n. The source restricts 0<q<1.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: Exact positive reciprocal-power errors C/k^p converge and are slower than every positive geometric BigO rate.
hypotheses: C>0, p>0, 0<q<1; source indices k>=1; limits are atTop.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: A polynomial upper bound alone does not establish the sublinear classification.
hypotheses: The exact counterexample is the identically zero error sequence, bounded by (n+1)^(-1) and geometric BigO.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: The quadratic convergence convention is the positive-constant inequality; sufficiently small nonnegative errors with that recurrence converge.
hypotheses: C>0; errors nonnegative; error(n+1)<=C*error(n)^2 for every n; C*error(0)<1 supplies the sufficient small-initial-error domain.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: Scalar Newton at a regular root of a C2 function has an invariant local domain, a positive quadratic constant and convergent actual iterates.
hypotheses: f:R->R is ContDiff R 2; f(root)=0; deriv f root !=0. The theorem derives radius>0 and coefficient>0 and assumes only |initial-root|<=radius for the iterates.

Fact — Formulas for the common induced norms
    
      For $m,n\ge1$, $\|A\|_1=\max_j\sum_i|a_{ij}|$ (largest absolute column sum); $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|a_{ij}|$ (largest absolute row sum); $\|A\|_2=\sigma_{\max}(A)=\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(A^\top A)}$, the spectral norm (Section 5); mixed: $\|A\|_{p\to\infty}=\max_i\|a_{i,:}\|_q$ with $\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q=1$ (e.g. $\|A\|_{2\to\infty}$ is the largest row length, $\|A\|_{1\to\infty}=\max_{ij}|a_{ij}|$) and $\|A\|_{1\to p}=\max_j\|a_{:,j}\|_p$.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: The induced 1 and infinity norms are the largest absolute column and row sums.
hypotheses: Arbitrary finite real rectangular matrix; the simultaneous source table assumes both row and column index types nonempty (m,n>=1).

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: The spectral norm is the largest actual singular value and square root of the largest actual Gram eigenvalue.
hypotheses: Finite real matrix with nonempty input index type; the source table supplies m,n>=1. Gram eigenvalues/nonnegativity and genuine singular-value correspondence are derived.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: For every conjugate p,q, the p-to-infinity norm is the largest row q-norm; 1-to-p is the largest column p-norm.
hypotheses: p,q:R>=0 extended, p,q>=1, ENNReal.HolderConjugate p q; endpoints 1 and infinity included. Arbitrary finite matrix; row/column nonemptiness follows from the new m,n>=1 table prefix.

hypotheses: Arbitrary finite real matrix with m,n>=1; sourcePNorm and sourceMatrixMap are the actual PiLp norms and linear map.

entire_current_literal.source_text: Proofs. $|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_j|a_{ij}|\,\|x\|_\infty$, attained by $x_j=\mathrm{sign}(a_{i^\star j})$ for the worst row $i^\star$. $\|Ax\|_1\le\sum_j|x_j|\sum_i|a_{ij}|$, attained at $x=e_{j^\star}$. Each output coordinate $a_{i,:}x$ is bounded by $\|a_{i,:}\|_q\|x\|_p$ (Hölder, attainable). $\square$ Running example $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2\\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$: $\|A\|_1=3$, $\|A\|_\infty=4$ (at $x=(1,1)$), $\|A\|_{1\to\infty}=2$, $\|A\|_{2\to\infty}=\sqrt8$, $\|A\|_2=2\sqrt2\approx2.83$: the longest semi-axis of the ellipse $A$ makes of the unit circle (Section 5, explorer).

entire_current_literal.source_text: The image of a box is a zonotope. For $\varepsilon>0$, $W$ maps $\{\|\delta\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\}$ to a sum of segments $\varepsilon[-w_j,w_j]$ over its columns (a parallelogram for invertible $2\times2$ $W$). The tightest enclosing box has half-widths $\varepsilon\|w_{i,:}\|_1$, which is what interval bound propagation keeps: for $W=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$, $\varepsilon=1$, the image is the square with corners $(\pm2,0),(0,\pm2)$, area $8$, inside the box $[-2,2]^2$ of area $16$.

hypotheses: Finite input index set, arbitrary real rectangular W; epsilon>0 in the source. The image/segment identities hold for epsilon>=0 and derive both set-inclusion directions.

hypotheses: Real2x2 W with det W !=0; epsilon>0 ensures scaled column generators remain independent.

hypotheses: Finite real W and epsilon>=0; arbitrary enclosing lower/upper endpoint vectors. Source epsilon>0 satisfies the domain; containment iff every endpoint bounds the derived extrema.

entire_current_literal.source_text: Covering numbers. Assume $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$ and $d\ge1$. A cube of side $s$ lies in the $\ell_2$ ball of radius $s\sqrt d/2$ about its centre. Cutting $[0,1]^d$ into $m^d$ cubes with $m=\lceil\sqrt d/(2\tau)\rceil$ covers it by $m^d$ balls of radius $\tau$; their centres form a $\tau$-net, and the fewest balls that suffice is the covering number $M(\tau,[0,1]^d)$. For $\tau=0.1$: $64$ balls in $d=2$, about $1.1\times10^{12}$ in $d=10$. If an $L$-Lipschitz function has margin $m_0$ at every net point, its margin is at least $m_0-L\tau$ everywhere (Primer B).

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: Every side-s cube about its actual center lies in the Euclidean ball of half-diagonal radius, including isometric images.
hypotheses: s>=0; finite coordinates; source d>=1. Coordinate deviations<=s/2; isometric image additionally has Isometry e.

hypotheses: d>=1 and tau>0; m=Nat.ceil(sqrt(d)/(2*tau)); actual center coordinates (k+1/2)/m; coverage and finite cardinality are derived.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: The covering number is the least finite ball count even when centers are permitted anywhere in the ambient space.
hypotheses: Finite-dimensional Euclidean unit cube and tau>0. Actual coordinate clipping maps any ambient finite cover to an in-cube net with no larger cardinality.

hypotheses: These are construction counts and covering-number upper bounds; no claim that the counts are minimal. Exact tau=1/10.

hypotheses: Pseudometric domain D, finite domain-contained tau-net Z, L>=0, LipschitzOnWith L f D, and f(z)>=m0 for every net point.

entire_current_literal.source_text: Signed distance and Hausdorff distance. For a closed set $C$ with $C\ne\emptyset$ and $C^c\ne\emptyset$, a signed distance equals $\mathrm{dist}(x,C)$ on one side of the boundary and $-\mathrm{dist}(x,\text{complement})$ on the other; which side is positive is a declared convention (reachability modules put the safe side positive). It vanishes on the boundary, so "$\ell\gt0$" and "$\ell\ge0$" differ exactly there. The Hausdorff distance $d_H(A,B)=\max\{\sup_{a\in A}\mathrm{dist}(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}\mathrm{dist}(b,A)\}$ compares nonempty compact sets, e.g. $d_H([0,1],[0,2])=1$.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: Signed distance equals distance to C outside and minus distance to the complement inside, with zero exactly at the boundary.
hypotheses: Metric space; C closed and nonempty with nonempty complement. Actual signedDistance=infDist(x,C)-infDist(x,C complement).

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: The safe-side-positive convention negates the sign; strict and nonstrict positive sign sets differ exactly on the boundary.
hypotheses: Same nonempty proper closed-set domain; safeSidePositiveDistance=-signedDistance; positivity inside means membership in interior C. This is a sign convention, with no trajectory safety theorem inferred.

hypotheses: A,B nonempty compact subsets of a metric space. Real finiteness and supremum boundedness are derived from compactness/nonemptiness.

entire_current_literal.source_text: Examples. $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ has positive entries, yet $x=(1,-1)$ gives $-2$: indefinite. $\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ gives $(x_1-x_2)^2\ge0$: PSD and singular. For diagonal matrices the notions agree: $T=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_i)\succeq0$ iff every $\lambda_i\ge0$. In the plane, the level sets $q=1$ are ellipses (PD), two parallel lines (nonzero singular PSD) or hyperbolas (indefinite); for the zero matrix this level set is empty: see the explorer.

hypotheses: Exact real matrices [[1,2],[2,1]] and [[1,-1],[-1,1]]; explicit positive/negative witnesses, nonzero/determinant and PSD properties are derived.

hypotheses: Real symmetric2x2 P with primitive positive-definite predicate. Actual eigenvector matrix is orthogonal, invertible and norm-preserving; semiaxes positivity is derived.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: In the plane a nonzero singular PSD matrix has exactly two distinct parallel one-level lines.
hypotheses: Real symmetric2x2 P, PSD, P!=0 and det P=0. The actual two eigenvalues are one positive and one zero; no rank conclusion is assumed.

all_subclaim_correspondence.source_clause: In the plane indefinite one-level sets are hyperbolas in actual orthogonal coordinates; the zero matrix one-level set is empty.
hypotheses: Real symmetric2x2 primitive indefinite P has witnesses of both signs. The exceptional zero matrix is treated separately; no higher-dimensional conic classification is asserted.
